claim: Fbxo24 is predominantly expressed in the testis among adult mouse tissues.
source: RT-PCR of Fbxo24 in mouse adult tissues. Fbxo24 is predominantly expressed in the testis.
evidence: RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1A demonstrates tissue-specific expression pattern.

claim: Fbxo24 expression increases around postnatal day 21 when round spermatids appear.
source: Fbxo24 signals increased after birth, with solid signals observed around postnatal day 21 (Figure 1B) when round spermatids appear (Kluin et al., 1982).
evidence: RT-PCR time course data and citation to published literature on spermatid appearance timing.

claim: Mouse Fbxo24 is expressed during post-meiotic stages of spermatogenesis.
source: Consistent with the RT-PCR results, single-cell transcriptome data (Hermann et al., 2018) indicates that mouse Fbxo24 and its human orthologue, FBXO24, are expressed during the post-meiotic stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Single-cell RNA-seq data from published dataset supports expression pattern.

claim: Human FBXO24 is expressed during post-meiotic stages of spermatogenesis.
source: Consistent with the RT-PCR results, single-cell transcriptome data (Hermann et al., 2018) indicates that mouse Fbxo24 and its human orthologue, FBXO24, are expressed during the post-meiotic stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Single-cell RNA-seq data from published dataset supports expression pattern.

claim: FBXO24 is highly conserved between mice and humans with 88% amino acid identity.
source: Pairwise sequence alignment of amino acids sequences revealed that FBXO24 is highly conserved between mice and humans (88% amino acid identity) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Sequence alignment analysis demonstrates conservation.

claim: The F-box domain of FBXO24 is located near the N-terminus.
source: Pairwise sequence alignment of amino acids sequences revealed that FBXO24 is highly conserved between mice and humans (88% amino acid identity) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) with the F-box domains located near the N-terminus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Domain analysis shown in figure identifies location.

claim: F-box proteins bind to SKP1 via the F-box domain to form the SCF complex.
source: Because it has been reported that F-box proteins bind to SKP1 via the F-box domain to form the SCF complex (Bai et al., 1996; Schulman et al., 2000), we investigated the interaction of FBXO24 with SKP1 by co-immunoprecipitation using HEK293T cells.
evidence: Statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Wild-type FBXO24 interacts with SKP1 via the F-box domain.
source: When SKP1-1D4 was immunoprecipitated with an anti-1D4 antibody, WT FBXO24-FLAG was co-immunoprecipitated, whereas ΔF FBXO24-FLAG was not (Figure 1D, left). Conversely, when an anti-FLAG antibody was used to immunoprecipitate WT or ΔF FBXO24-FLAG, SKP1-1D4 was co-immunoprecipitated only with WT FBXO24-FLAG (Figure 1D, right).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate interaction dependent on F-box domain.

claim: FBXO24 lacking the F-box domain does not interact with SKP1.
source: When SKP1-1D4 was immunoprecipitated with an anti-1D4 antibody, WT FBXO24-FLAG was co-immunoprecipitated, whereas ΔF FBXO24-FLAG was not (Figure 1D, left). Conversely, when an anti-FLAG antibody was used to immunoprecipitate WT or ΔF FBXO24-FLAG, SKP1-1D4 was co-immunoprecipitated only with WT FBXO24-FLAG (Figure 1D, right).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments show loss of interaction without F-box domain.

claim: FBXO24 could function as a component of the SCF complex in mouse testis during post-meiotic stages of spermatogenesis.
source: These results suggest that FBXO24 could function as a component of the SCF complex in mouse testis, during the post-meiotic stages of spermatogenesis.
evidence: Inference based on interaction data and expression pattern.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout mice were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 with an 11,575 bp deletion.
source: We performed genomic PCR using the primers described in Figure 1E and F and confirmed that Fbxo24 KO mice had a deletion of 11,575 bp by Sanger sequencing (Figure 1G).
evidence: Sequencing data confirms the deletion size.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout male mice are completely infertile.
source: Although 20 vaginal plugs were detected, no pups were born from the Fbxo24 KO male mice (Figure 1H), suggesting that Fbxo24 is indispensable for male fertility.
evidence: Fertility test data shows zero offspring from KO males.

claim: Fbxo24 is indispensable for male fertility.
source: Although 20 vaginal plugs were detected, no pups were born from the Fbxo24 KO male mice (Figure 1H), suggesting that Fbxo24 is indispensable for male fertility.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from fertility test results.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout mice show no overt gross defects in development, behavior, or survival.
source: We found no overt gross defects in development, behavior, or survival in Fbxo24 KO mice.
evidence: Observational data from mouse phenotyping.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout mice have normal testicular morphology and weights.
source: No apparent differences in gross testicular morphology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) or weights (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) were found between controls and Fbxo24 KO mice.
evidence: Morphological and weight measurements show no differences.

claim: Spermiation is impaired in Fbxo24 knockout testes.
source: Although elongating spermatids can be found in Fbxo24 KO testes, step 16 spermatids were still present in Stage IX seminiferous tubules (Figure 2A), indicating that spermiation was impaired in Fbxo24 KO testes.
evidence: Histological analysis shows retained spermatids at inappropriate stage.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa exhibit abnormal tail structures including bent or coiled flagella.
source: While KO spermatozoa showed comparable head morphology to the controls, KO spermatozoa exhibited abnormal tail structures such as bent or coiled flagella (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Morphological analysis of spermatozoa shows flagellar defects.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa have normal head morphology.
source: While KO spermatozoa showed comparable head morphology to the controls, KO spermatozoa exhibited abnormal tail structures such as bent or coiled flagella (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Morphological comparison shows no head defects.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa show no overt abnormalities in acrosome or nucleus.
source: Further analyses of sperm head morphology with immunostaining showed no overt abnormalities in the acrosome or nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Immunostaining analysis shows normal acrosome and nuclear structures.

claim: The percentage of motile spermatozoa is significantly reduced in Fbxo24 knockout mice.
source: CASA revealed that the percentages of motile spermatozoa were significantly reduced in Fbxo24 KO mice compared to the controls (Figure 2D and Figure 2—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Computer-assisted sperm analysis provides quantitative motility data.

claim: All velocity parameters (VAP, VSL, VCL) are lower in Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: Furthermore, all velocity parameters such as average path velocity, straight line velocity, and curvilinear velocity were lower in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: CASA measurements show reduced velocity across all parameters.

claim: FBXO24 is critical in sperm flagellum formation during spermiogenesis.
source: These results indicate that FBXO24 is critical in sperm flagellum formation during spermiogenesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from flagellar morphology and motility defects.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa cannot fertilize eggs in vitro.
source: Consistent with male sterility observed in vivo (Figure 1H), Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa could not fertilize eggs in vitro (Figure 3A).
evidence: IVF experiments show zero fertilization rate.

claim: Removing cumulus cells does not rescue fertilization rates of Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: Furthermore, removing cumulus cells (Figure 3B) or both cumulus cells and the ZP (Figure 3C) could not rescue the fertilization rates
evidence: IVF experiments with cumulus-free oocytes show no improvement.

claim: Removing both cumulus cells and zona pellucida does not rescue fertilization rates of Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: Furthermore, removing cumulus cells (Figure 3B) or both cumulus cells and the ZP (Figure 3C) could not rescue the fertilization rates
evidence: IVF experiments with zona-free oocytes show no improvement.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa may have defects in both sperm motility and the acrosome reaction.
source: Furthermore, removing cumulus cells (Figure 3B) or both cumulus cells and the ZP (Figure 3C) could not rescue the fertilization rates, suggesting that Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa may have defects in not only sperm motility but also the acrosome reaction, which is a prerequisite for spermatozoa to pass through the ZP and fuse with eggs (Morohoshi et al., 2023).
evidence: Inference from IVF results with different oocyte preparations and citation to acrosome reaction requirement.

claim: The acrosome reaction is a prerequisite for spermatozoa to pass through the zona pellucida and fuse with eggs.
source: Furthermore, removing cumulus cells (Figure 3B) or both cumulus cells and the ZP (Figure 3C) could not rescue the fertilization rates, suggesting that Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa may have defects in not only sperm motility but also the acrosome reaction, which is a prerequisite for spermatozoa to pass through the ZP and fuse with eggs (Morohoshi et al., 2023).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The percentage of dead spermatozoa is significantly higher in Fbxo24 knockout mice.
source: First, to test whether Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa were viable, we performed propidium iodide (PI) staining and found that the percentages of dead spermatozoa were significantly higher in Fbxo24 KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: PI staining data shows increased dead sperm in KO.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa rarely undergo the acrosome reaction even after Ca2+ ionophore treatment.
source: While the control spermatozoa underwent the acrosome reaction after 120 min of incubation in capacitation medium and with Ca2+ ionophore (A23187) treatment, Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa rarely underwent the acrosome reaction even after adding A23187 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Acrosome reaction assay shows impaired response to ionophore.

claim: No notable differences were found in SNARE-related proteins between control and Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: Since the SNARE complex is considered critical for the acrosome reaction (Hutt et al., 2005; Katafuchi et al., 2000; Schulz et al., 1997; Tomes et al., 2002), we examined the amounts of SNARE-related proteins in mature spermatozoa using mass spectrometry (MS) and immunoblotting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), but no notable differences were found in SNARE-related proteins between the control and Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa.
evidence: MS and immunoblotting data show comparable SNARE protein levels.

claim: The SNARE complex is critical for the acrosome reaction.
source: Since the SNARE complex is considered critical for the acrosome reaction (Hutt et al., 2005; Katafuchi et al., 2000; Schulz et al., 1997; Tomes et al., 2002), we examined the amounts of SNARE-related proteins in mature spermatozoa using mass spectrometry (MS) and immunoblotting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), but no notable differences were found in SNARE-related proteins between the control and Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa.
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: No significant differences were found in PLCD4 between control and Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: Further, no significant differences were found in PLCD4 that has been reported to be important for the acrosome reaction (Fukami et al., 2001).
evidence: MS data shows comparable PLCD4 levels.

claim: PLCD4 is important for the acrosome reaction.
source: Further, no significant differences were found in PLCD4 that has been reported to be important for the acrosome reaction (Fukami et al., 2001).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa hardly pass through the uterotubal junction 4 hours after mating.
source: Although the control spermatozoa migrate through the uterotubal junction (UTJ) 4 hr after mating, Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa hardly passed through the UTJ (Figure 3D).
evidence: In vivo migration assay shows impaired UTJ passage.

claim: ADAM3 is processed correctly in Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: Since the processing of sperm membrane protein, ADAM3, is necessary for sperm migration through the UTJ (Fujihara et al., 2019; Yamaguchi et al., 2006), we performed immunoblotting analyses and found that ADAM3 was processed correctly even in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa (Figure 3E).
evidence: Immunoblotting shows normal ADAM3 processing.

claim: Processing of ADAM3 is necessary for sperm migration through the uterotubal junction.
source: Since the processing of sperm membrane protein, ADAM3, is necessary for sperm migration through the UTJ (Fujihara et al., 2019; Yamaguchi et al., 2006), we performed immunoblotting analyses and found that ADAM3 was processed correctly even in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa (Figure 3E).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: No significant differences in LY6K amounts were detected between control and Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: We further performed immunoblotting of LY6K because Ly6k KO spermatozoa cannot migrate through the UTJ even with normal ADAM3 processing (Fujihara et al., 2014). However, we did not detect significant differences in the amounts of LY6K (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Immunoblotting shows comparable LY6K levels.

claim: Ly6k knockout spermatozoa cannot migrate through the uterotubal junction even with normal ADAM3 processing.
source: We further performed immunoblotting of LY6K because Ly6k KO spermatozoa cannot migrate through the UTJ even with normal ADAM3 processing (Fujihara et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The acrosome reaction is not essential for sperm migration in the female reproductive tract.
source: Considering that the acrosome reaction is not essential for sperm migration in the female reproductive tract (Morohoshi et al., 2023) and defects in sperm motility could cause impaired migration through the UTJ (Chung et al., 2014; Fujihara et al., 2018; Miyata et al., 2015; Shimada et al., 2019), these results suggest that lower viability and decreased sperm motility can be the cause of abnormal sperm migration and male sterility in vivo.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Defects in sperm motility can cause impaired migration through the uterotubal junction.
source: Considering that the acrosome reaction is not essential for sperm migration in the female reproductive tract (Morohoshi et al., 2023) and defects in sperm motility could cause impaired migration through the UTJ (Chung et al., 2014; Fujihara et al., 2018; Miyata et al., 2015; Shimada et al., 2019), these results suggest that lower viability and decreased sperm motility can be the cause of abnormal sperm migration and male sterility in vivo.
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Lower viability and decreased sperm motility can be the cause of abnormal sperm migration and male sterility in Fbxo24 knockout mice.
source: Considering that the acrosome reaction is not essential for sperm migration in the female reproductive tract (Morohoshi et al., 2023) and defects in sperm motility could cause impaired migration through the UTJ (Chung et al., 2014; Fujihara et al., 2018; Miyata et al., 2015; Shimada et al., 2019), these results suggest that lower viability and decreased sperm motility can be the cause of abnormal sperm migration and male sterility in vivo.
evidence: Inference drawn from viability, motility, and migration data combined with literature.

claim: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection can rescue male sterility of Fbxo24 knockout mice.
source: These results indicate that ICSI can rescue male sterility of Fbxo24 KO mice.
evidence: ICSI experiments produced viable offspring from KO sperm.

claim: Fbxo24 knockout sperm nuclei have the potential to generate the next generation.
source: Next, we performed intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) to examine whether nuclei of Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa have the potential to generate the next generation. We injected Fbxo24 KO sperm heads into 91 WT oocytes, and obtained 48 two-cell stage embryos (Figure 3F). By transplanting the two-cell embryos into the oviduct of pseudopregnant ICR females, we obtained four pups, which were confirmed to have the heterozygous mutation by PCR (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: ICSI produced viable offspring confirming nuclear competence.

claim: Mitochondria are disorganized in Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: We observed midpieces using RBGS Tg mice and revealed that mitochondria were disorganized in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa (Figure 4A).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy of mitochondrial marker shows disorganization.

claim: SEPT4 localizes to the proper region in Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: We also observed SEPT4, a component of the annulus (Kissel et al., 2005), and found that SEPT4 localized to the proper region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Immunostaining shows normal SEPT4 localization.

claim: SEPT4 is a component of the annulus.
source: We also observed SEPT4, a component of the annulus (Kissel et al., 2005), and found that SEPT4 localized to the proper region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Spherical mitochondria align correctly in early steps of mitochondrial sheath formation in both control and Fbxo24 knockout spermatids.
source: During the early step of mitochondrial sheath formation, mitochondria wrap around the axoneme. In both control and Fbxo24 KO spermatids, spherical mitochondria were aligned correctly at this step (Figure 4B, left panels).
evidence: SEM observation shows normal early alignment.

claim: Irregular interlocking of mitochondria is observed in Fbxo24 knockout spermatids during mitochondrial sheath formation.
source: In the next step, mitochondria became crescent-shaped and were interlocked in the control spermatids, whereas irregular interlocking was observed in Fbxo24 KO spermatids (Figure 4B, middle panels).
evidence: SEM observation shows abnormal interlocking in KO.

claim: Elongating mitochondria remain irregularly arranged in Fbxo24 knockout spermatids.
source: Subsequently, elongating mitochondria remain irregularly arranged in Fbxo24 KO spermatids (Figure 4B, right panels).
evidence: SEM observation shows persistent irregular arrangement.

claim: Mitochondria are irregularly arranged in Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa as observed by transmission electron microscopy.
source: To further investigate the morphological abnormality of the midpiece in Fbxo24 KO mice, we observed the ultrastructure of the cauda epididymal spermatozoa using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Consistent with the SEM results, we found that mitochondria were irregularly arranged in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: TEM observation confirms irregular mitochondrial arrangement.

claim: The frequency of abnormal mitochondria is significantly higher in Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: The frequency of abnormal mitochondria was significantly higher in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa (Figure 4E).
evidence: Quantification of TEM images shows increased abnormality frequency.

claim: The axoneme and outer dense fibers are disrupted in both midpieces and principal pieces of Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: In addition, the axoneme and ODF were disrupted in both midpieces and principal pieces of Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: TEM observation shows structural disruptions.

claim: Numerous membraneless electron-dense granules are frequently observed in the midpieces of Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: Furthermore, we frequently observed numerous membraneless electron-dense granules in the midpieces of Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa (Figure 4C, D, and F).
evidence: TEM observation shows presence of granules.

claim: Membraneless electron-dense granules are found even in the axoneme of Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: We found these granules even in the axoneme (Figure 4C).
evidence: TEM observation shows granules within axoneme.

claim: Membraneless electron-dense granules are found in the principal pieces of Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa at low frequency.
source: Despite the low frequency, we also found membraneless electron-dense granules in the principal pieces of Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: TEM observation shows granules in principal piece.

claim: No differences in the amounts of RNP granule-related proteins (ADAD1, ADAD2, MILI, MIWI, RNF-17, YTHDC2, TSKS, TSSK1) were found between Fbxo24 heterozygous and knockout testes.
source: Because membraneless electron-dense granules accumulated in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa, we examined RNP granule-related proteins in Fbxo24 KO mice. We performed immunoblotting analyses for ADAD1, ADAD2, MILI, MIWI, RNF-17, YTHDC2, TSKS, and TSSK1, which localized in germ-cell RNP granules and are essential for spermatogenesis (Lu et al., 2023; Meikar et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2005; Shang et al., 2010; Shimada et al., 2023; Snyder et al., 2020), but we did not see any differences in the amounts of these proteins between Fbxo24 heterozygous and KO testes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Immunoblotting shows comparable protein levels.

claim: ADAD1, ADAD2, MILI, MIWI, RNF-17, YTHDC2, TSKS, and TSSK1 localize in germ-cell RNP granules and are essential for spermatogenesis.
source: We performed immunoblotting analyses for ADAD1, ADAD2, MILI, MIWI, RNF-17, YTHDC2, TSKS, and TSSK1, which localized in germ-cell RNP granules and are essential for spermatogenesis (Lu et al., 2023; Meikar et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2005; Shang et al., 2010; Shimada et al., 2023; Snyder et al., 2020), but we did not see any differences in the amounts of these proteins between Fbxo24 heterozygous and KO testes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: No abnormalities in the localization of MIWI were found in Fbxo24 knockout testes.
source: Further, we found no abnormalities in the localization of MIWI in Fbxo24 KO testes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Immunostaining shows normal MIWI localization pattern.

claim: MIWI localizes in intermitochondrial cement of late spermatocytes and chromatoid bodies of round spermatids and disappears in elongating spermatids.
source: MIWI was localized in the IMCs of late spermatocytes and CBs of round spermatids and disappeared in elongating spermatids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Immunostaining shows stage-specific MIWI localization.

claim: No abnormalities in the immunostaining of TSKS were found in Fbxo24 knockout testes.
source: Further, no abnormalities were found in the immunostaining of TSKS, which localized in the reticulated body and CB remnant of elongating spermatids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Immunostaining shows normal TSKS localization.

claim: TSKS localizes in the reticulated body and chromatoid body remnant of elongating spermatids.
source: Further, no abnormalities were found in the immunostaining of TSKS, which localized in the reticulated body and CB remnant of elongating spermatids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Immunostaining shows TSKS localization pattern.

claim: Loss of F-box protein causes accumulation of substrates.
source: Since previous studies show that loss of F-box protein causes the accumulation of substrates (Nakayama et al., 2000; Tsunematsu et al., 2004), we investigated whether certain proteins accumulated in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The amounts of IPO5 and KPNB1 significantly increase in Fbxo24 knockout mature spermatozoa.
source: MS analyses revealed that the amounts of several proteins significantly increased in Fbxo24 KO mature spermatozoa (Figure 5A). Among the significantly increased proteins, we focused on IPO5 (importin 5, also known as KPNB3 and RanBP5) and KPNB1 (karyopherin subunit beta 1, also known as importin β1) because the fold changes (KO/WT) are the highest in these two proteins.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shows increased protein levels.

claim: IPO5 and KPNB1 are members of the karyopherin-β family of nuclear transport receptors.
source: Both IPO5 and KPNB1 are members of the karyopherin-β (KPNB) family of nuclear transport receptors (NTRs), which play a crucial role in nucleocytoplasmic transport (Chook and Blobel, 2001; Chook and Süel, 2011; Conti and Izaurralde, 2001; Kimura and Imamoto, 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Karyopherin-β family of nuclear transport receptors play a crucial role in nucleocytoplasmic transport.
source: Both IPO5 and KPNB1 are members of the karyopherin-β (KPNB) family of nuclear transport receptors (NTRs), which play a crucial role in nucleocytoplasmic transport (Chook and Blobel, 2001; Chook and Süel, 2011; Conti and Izaurralde, 2001; Kimura and Imamoto, 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In rodent testes, KPNB1 localizes to the cytoplasm of spermatogonia, spermatocytes, and Sertoli cells.
source: In rodent testes, KPNB1 localized to the cytoplasm of spermatogonia, spermatocytes, and Sertoli cells, and IPO5 localized to the cytoplasm of elongating spermatids (Loveland et al., 2015; Loveland et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In rodent testes, IPO5 localizes to the cytoplasm of elongating spermatids.
source: In rodent testes, KPNB1 localized to the cytoplasm of spermatogonia, spermatocytes, and Sertoli cells, and IPO5 localized to the cytoplasm of elongating spermatids (Loveland et al., 2015; Loveland et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Immunoblotting confirmed that the amounts of IPO5 and KPNB1 increased in Fbxo24 knockout mature spermatozoa.
source: Immunoblotting analyses confirmed that the amounts of IPO5 and KPNB1 increased in Fbxo24 KO mature spermatozoa (Figure 5B).
evidence: Immunoblotting validates mass spectrometry findings.

claim: The amounts of KPNA2 are comparable between control and Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: In contrast, the amounts of KPNA2 (importin α1), a member of karyopherin-α (KPNA) family of NTRs which localized to the cytoplasm and nucleus of spermatocytes and the cytoplasm of elongating spermatids (Miyamoto et al., 2013), were comparable between the control and Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa.
evidence: Immunoblotting shows no change in KPNA2 levels.

claim: KPNA2 is a member of karyopherin-α family of nuclear transport receptors that localizes to the cytoplasm and nucleus of spermatocytes and the cytoplasm of elongating spermatids.
source: In contrast, the amounts of KPNA2 (importin α1), a member of karyopherin-α (KPNA) family of NTRs which localized to the cytoplasm and nucleus of spermatocytes and the cytoplasm of elongating spermatids (Miyamoto et al., 2013), were comparable between the control and Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: IPO5 is detected in Fbxo24 knockout flagella but not in control flagella.
source: Since the anti-KPNB1 antibody did not work for immunostaining, we performed immunostaining of mature spermatozoa using an anti-IPO5 antibody. We detected IPO5 in the Fbxo24 KO flagella but not in control (Figure 5C).
evidence: Immunostaining shows IPO5 accumulation in KO flagella.

claim: FBXO24 can interact with IPO5 in mouse testes.
source: Using Tg mice, we could immunoprecipitate FBXO24-FLAG with an anti-FLAG antibody, and subsequent MS analyses detected not only FBXO24 but also IPO5 with the highest quantitative values (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H), indicating that these proteins interact in vivo. We also found SKP1 in this analysis, consistent with the in vitro study (Figure 1D). We confirmed that IPO5 co-immunoprecipitated with FBXO24-FLAG in mouse testes using immunoblotting analysis (Figure 5D).
evidence: Immunoprecipitation-MS and immunoblotting show protein interaction.

claim: FBXO24 can interact with endogenous IPO5 but not with endogenous KPNB1 in HEK293T cells.
source: Further, we transiently expressed 3×FLAG-tagged Fbxo24 in HEK293T cells, performed immunoprecipitation analysis using an anti-FLAG antibody, and found that FBXO24 could interact with endogenous IPO5 but not with endogenous KPNB1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Immunoprecipitation in cultured cells shows selective interaction.

claim: FBXO24 can ubiquitinate IPO5.
source: To examine if FBXO24 can ubiquitinate IPO5, we performed a ubiquitination assay using HEK293T cells and revealed that ubiquitination of IPO5 was upregulated when cells were transfected with WT FBXO24, but not with ΔF FBXO24 that lacks the F-box domain (Figure 5F).
evidence: Ubiquitination assay shows FBXO24-dependent ubiquitination of IPO5.

claim: FBXO24 lacking the F-box domain cannot ubiquitinate IPO5.
source: To examine if FBXO24 can ubiquitinate IPO5, we performed a ubiquitination assay using HEK293T cells and revealed that ubiquitination of IPO5 was upregulated when cells were transfected with WT FBXO24, but not with ΔF FBXO24 that lacks the F-box domain (Figure 5F).
evidence: Ubiquitination assay shows F-box domain requirement.

claim: FBXO24 recognizes and ubiquitinates IPO5 for subsequent protein degradation.
source: These results suggest that FBXO24 recognizes and ubiquitinates IPO5 for subsequent protein degradation.
evidence: Inference from interaction and ubiquitination data.

claim: The total amount of RNAs is significantly increased in Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: In contrast, the total amount of RNAs was significantly increased in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa (Figure 6A and B)
evidence: RNA quantification shows increased RNA levels in KO.

claim: Various stresses such as heat shock, arsenite treatment, or proteasome inhibition trigger the formation of cytoplasmic stress granules.
source: Previous studies showed that various stresses, such as heat shock, arsenite treatment, or proteasome inhibition, trigger the formation of cytoplasmic stress granules (SGs), membraneless granules composed of RNPs.
evidence: Statement based on prior literature knowledge.

claim: Stress granules can contain KPNB1.
source: Further, it has been shown that SGs could contain KPNB1 (Chang and Tarn, 2009; Mahboubi et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: IPO5 is predominantly localized to the cytoplasm in COS7 cells without stress inducer.
source: We examined the subcellular localization of endogenous IPO5 and KPNB1 in COS7 cells treated with arsenite, an oxidative stress inducer. Immunostaining analyses revealed that IPO5 was predominantly localized to the cytoplasm without the stress inducer (Figure 6C)
evidence: Immunostaining shows baseline IPO5 localization.

claim: When COS7 cells are treated with arsenite, IPO5 is detected in cytoplasmic granules that colocalize with KPNB1.
source: Immunostaining analyses revealed that IPO5 was predominantly localized to the cytoplasm without the stress inducer (Figure 6C); however, when cells were treated with arsenite, IPO5 was detected not only in the cytoplasm but also in cytoplasmic granules that were colocalized with KPNB1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Immunostaining shows stress-induced granule formation with colocalization.

claim: MG132 causes the accumulation of cytoplasmic granules that contain IPO5 and KPNB1 in COS7 cells.
source: We then analyzed if the stress of proteasome inhibition could cause a similar response. We performed immunostaining of IPO5 and KPNB1 in COS7 cells using a proteasome inhibitor, MG132. Consistent with arsenite, MG132 caused the accumulation of cytoplasmic granules that contained IPO5 and KPNB1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Immunostaining shows proteasome inhibitor-induced granule formation.

claim: RNP granules that contain KPNB1 and IPO5 are formed in Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa.
source: These results support the idea that RNP granules that contain KPNB1 and IPO5 are formed in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa.
evidence: Inference from stress granule experiments and KO phenotype.

claim: Protein ubiquitination by the ubiquitin-proteasome system is involved in various physiological phenomena such as cell cycle regulation and signal transduction.
source: Ubiquitinated proteins are degraded by a ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), which is involved in various physiological phenomena in cells, such as cell cycle regulation and signal transduction (Ciechanover and Schwartz, 1998; Mani and Gelmann, 2005; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Approximately 600 E3 ligase genes are estimated to be present in humans.
source: Among the approximately 600 E3 ligase genes estimated to be present in humans (Li et al., 2008), the mechanism and functions of ubiquitination mediated by the SCF (Skp1-Cul1-F-box protein) complex has been well studied (Skaar et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The mechanism and functions of ubiquitination mediated by the SCF complex has been well studied.
source: Among the approximately 600 E3 ligase genes estimated to be present in humans (Li et al., 2008), the mechanism and functions of ubiquitination mediated by the SCF (Skp1-Cul1-F-box protein) complex has been well studied (Skaar et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The SCF complex consists of SKP1, a cullin protein, an F-box protein, and RBX1.
source: The SCF complex consists of several proteins such as SKP1, a cullin protein, an F-box protein, and RBX1, and can ubiquitinate various substrates by using different F-box proteins that recognize distinct substrates.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of SCF complex.

claim: The SCF complex can ubiquitinate various substrates by using different F-box proteins that recognize distinct substrates.
source: The SCF complex consists of several proteins such as SKP1, a cullin protein, an F-box protein, and RBX1, and can ubiquitinate various substrates by using different F-box proteins that recognize distinct substrates.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of SCF complex function.

claim: At least 38 F-box proteins have been identified in humans.
source: In humans, at least 38 F-box proteins have been identified, but the functions of most F-box proteins remain unclear (Kipreos and Pagano, 2000).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The functions of most F-box proteins remain unclear.
source: In humans, at least 38 F-box proteins have been identified, but the functions of most F-box proteins remain unclear (Kipreos and Pagano, 2000).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: FBXO24 is essential for sperm flagellum formation and male fertility.
source: In this study, we analyzed the function of Fbxo24 (F-box protein 24), predominantly expressed in testes, and found that FXBO24 is essential for sperm flagellum formation and male fertility.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from KO mouse phenotype analysis.

claim: Ribonucleoprotein granules are membraneless electron-dense structures that assemble through liquid-liquid phase separation.
source: Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules are membraneless electron-dense structures that assemble through liquid–liquid phase separation and play critical roles in spermatogenesis (Eddy, 1974).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: RNP granules play critical roles in spermatogenesis.
source: Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules are membraneless electron-dense structures that assemble through liquid–liquid phase separation and play critical roles in spermatogenesis (Eddy, 1974).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Intermitochondrial cement and chromatoid body are involved in the piRNA pathway.
source: Among the RNP granules, intermitochondrial cement (IMC) observed in late spermatocytes and the chromatoid body (CB) found in round spermatids are involved in the PIWI-interacting RNA (piRNA) pathway (Meikar et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Intermitochondrial cement is observed in late spermatocytes.
source: Among the RNP granules, intermitochondrial cement (IMC) observed in late spermatocytes and the chromatoid body (CB) found in round spermatids are involved in the PIWI-interacting RNA (piRNA) pathway (Meikar et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Chromatoid body is found in round spermatids.
source: Among the RNP granules, intermitochondrial cement (IMC) observed in late spermatocytes and the chromatoid body (CB) found in round spermatids are involved in the PIWI-interacting RNA (piRNA) pathway (Meikar et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: After meiosis, intermitochondrial cement is no longer detectable because of mitochondrial dispersion.
source: After meiosis, IMCs are no longer detectable because of mitochondrial dispersion, and CBs become gradually larger in round spermatids.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of spermatogenesis.

claim: Chromatoid bodies become gradually larger in round spermatids.
source: After meiosis, IMCs are no longer detectable because of mitochondrial dispersion, and CBs become gradually larger in round spermatids.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of spermatogenesis.

claim: In elongating spermatids, chromatoid bodies containing MIWI disappear and reticulated body and CB remnant appear.
source: In elongating spermatids, the CBs containing MIWI, the main effector protein of the piRNA pathway, disappear and two other RNP structures called a reticulated body and a CB remnant that contain TSKS, TSSK1, and TSSK2 appear (Shang et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: MIWI is the main effector protein of the piRNA pathway.
source: In elongating spermatids, the CBs containing MIWI, the main effector protein of the piRNA pathway, disappear and two other RNP structures called a reticulated body and a CB remnant that contain TSKS, TSSK1, and TSSK2 appear (Shang et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Reticulated body and CB remnant contain TSKS, TSSK1, and TSSK2.
source: In elongating spermatids, the CBs containing MIWI, the main effector protein of the piRNA pathway, disappear and two other RNP structures called a reticulated body and a CB remnant that contain TSKS, TSSK1, and TSSK2 appear (Shang et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Tsks knockout mice fail to generate reticulated bodies and CB remnants and are infertile with impaired cytoplasmic removal.
source: Recently, we found that Tsks knockout (KO) mice failed to generate reticulated bodies and CB remnants, and were infertile with impaired cytoplasmic removal (Shimada et al., 2023), indicating that the formation and disassembly of RNP granules is highly regulated and important for spermiogenesis.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The formation and disassembly of RNP granules is highly regulated and important for spermiogenesis.
source: Recently, we found that Tsks knockout (KO) mice failed to generate reticulated bodies and CB remnants, and were infertile with impaired cytoplasmic removal (Shimada et al., 2023), indicating that the formation and disassembly of RNP granules is highly regulated and important for spermiogenesis.
evidence: Inference drawn from Tsks KO phenotype and citation.

claim: During spermiogenesis, post-translational modifications of proteins are critical since gene transcription is thought to cease with nuclear condensation.
source: During spermiogenesis, post-translational modifications of proteins are critical since gene transcription is thought to cease with nuclear condensation.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of spermiogenesis.

claim: Abnormal formation of flagellar structures could lead to male infertility.
source: Abnormal formation of these flagellar structures could lead to male infertility (Nsota Mbango et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The sperm flagellum is divided into three parts: midpiece, principal piece, and endpiece.
source: The motility apparatus of spermatozoa is the flagellum which is divided into three parts, a midpiece, a principal piece, and an endpiece, in order from proximal to distal (Eddy et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The midpiece contains the mitochondrial sheath and outer dense fibers surrounding the axoneme.
source: The midpiece contains accessory structures called the mitochondrial sheath and outer dense fibers (ODFs) that surround the axoneme, a 9+2 arrangement of microtubules, while the principal piece contains a different accessory structure called the fibrous sheath and ODFs surrounding the axoneme.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of sperm structure with citation.

claim: The principal piece contains the fibrous sheath and outer dense fibers surrounding the axoneme.
source: The midpiece contains accessory structures called the mitochondrial sheath and outer dense fibers (ODFs) that surround the axoneme, a 9+2 arrangement of microtubules, while the principal piece contains a different accessory structure called the fibrous sheath and ODFs surrounding the axoneme.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of sperm structure.

claim: The endpiece contains no accessory structures but the axoneme.
source: In contrast, the endpiece contains no accessory structures but the axoneme.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of sperm structure.

claim: The axoneme has a 9+2 arrangement of microtubules.
source: The midpiece contains accessory structures called the mitochondrial sheath and outer dense fibers (ODFs) that surround the axoneme, a 9+2 arrangement of microtubules, while the principal piece contains a different accessory structure called the fibrous sheath and ODFs surrounding the axoneme.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge of axoneme structure.

claim: Abnormal accumulation of proteins including IPO5 and KPNB1 may lead to morphological abnormalities in sperm flagella.
source: Abnormal accumulation of proteins, including IPO5 and KPNB1, may lead to morphological abnormalities in sperm flagella since the SCF complex is critical for protein degradation and consequently regulate various cellular processes (Skaar et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference from protein accumulation data and SCF complex function.

claim: The SCF complex is critical for protein degradation and consequently regulates various cellular processes.
source: Abnormal accumulation of proteins, including IPO5 and KPNB1, may lead to morphological abnormalities in sperm flagella since the SCF complex is critical for protein degradation and consequently regulate various cellular processes (Skaar et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: FBXO24 likely plays a role in catalyzing protein degradation during spermiogenesis.
source: FBXO24 likely plays a role in catalyzing protein degradation during spermiogenesis.
evidence: Inference from FBXO24 function and expression pattern.

claim: FBXO24 may degrade IPO5 in the testis.
source: Because we found that FBXO24 could interact with IPO5 in testes and catalyze ubiquitination of IPO5, FBXO24 may degrade IPO5 in the testis.
evidence: Inference from interaction and ubiquitination data.

claim: Mice lacking both PSME4 and ECPAS exhibit impaired male fertility with disorganized mitochondrial sheath but without numerous membraneless granules.
source: Recently, mice lacking both PSME4 and ECPAS, proteasome-associated proteins, were shown to exhibit impaired male fertility with disorganized mitochondrial sheath, but numerous membraneless granules were not observed (Sato et al., 2023), suggesting that the accumulation of the granules is specific to Fbxo24 deletion rather than simply caused by proteasome defects.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The accumulation of granules in Fbxo24 knockout is specific to Fbxo24 deletion rather than simply caused by proteasome defects.
source: Recently, mice lacking both PSME4 and ECPAS, proteasome-associated proteins, were shown to exhibit impaired male fertility with disorganized mitochondrial sheath, but numerous membraneless granules were not observed (Sato et al., 2023), suggesting that the accumulation of the granules is specific to Fbxo24 deletion rather than simply caused by proteasome defects.
evidence: Inference from comparison with other proteasome-related KO mice.

claim: The electron-dense granules accumulated in Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa may consist of RNPs.
source: In addition to proteins, the total RNA amount increased in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa, suggesting that the abnormal granules observed in Fbxo24 KO flagella may consist of RNPs.
evidence: Inference from increased RNA and protein accumulation.

claim: The electron-dense granules accumulated in Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa are different from well-studied RNP granules like IMC, CB, reticulated body, and CB remnant.
source: RNP granules are membraneless electron-dense structures that are similar to the abnormal granules in Fbxo24 KO; however, the localization of MIWI, an IMC and CB marker, and TSKS, a reticulated body and CB remnant marker, was not disrupted in the KO. These results suggest that electron-dense granules accumulated in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa are different from well-studied RNP granules.
evidence: Inference from normal localization of known RNP granule markers.

claim: Stress granules are membraneless electron-dense granules that contain RNPs and assemble through liquid-liquid phase separation in response to cellular stresses.
source: SGs are also membraneless electron-dense granules that contain RNPs, which assemble through liquid–liquid phase separation in response to cellular stresses (Buchan and Parker, 2009; Protter and Parker, 2016; Taylor et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Transient stress granules formed in response to oxidative stress or heat shock play roles in translational arrest to ensure cell survival.
source: While transient SGs formed in response to oxidative stress or heat shock play roles in translational arrest to ensure cell survival, chronic SGs are relevant to neurodegenerative diseases (Marcelo et al., 2021; Reineke and Neilson, 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Chronic stress granules are relevant to neurodegenerative diseases.
source: While transient SGs formed in response to oxidative stress or heat shock play roles in translational arrest to ensure cell survival, chronic SGs are relevant to neurodegenerative diseases (Marcelo et al., 2021; Reineke and Neilson, 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Under arsenite-induced oxidative stress, KPNB1 relocates to stress granules.
source: It has been shown that, under arsenite-induced oxidative stress, KPNB1 relocates to SGs (Chang and Tarn, 2009; Mahboubi et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Electron-dense granules observed in Fbxo24 knockout spermatozoa may be RNP granules consisting of IPO5 and KPNB1.
source: Because we found that not only KPNB1 but also IPO5 can be recruited to SGs after arsenite or proteasome inhibitor treatment, electron-dense granules observed in Fbxo24 KO spermatozoa may be RNP granules consisting of IPO5 and KPNB1.
evidence: Inference from stress granule experiments showing IPO5 and KPNB1 recruitment.

claim: FBXO24 is responsible for degrading proteins such as IPO5, which may prevent the accumulation of abnormal RNP granules.
source: Our results suggest that FBXO24 is responsible for degrading proteins such as IPO5, which may prevent the accumulation of abnormal RNP granules.
evidence: Inference from ubiquitination data and KO phenotype.

claim: Another group reported that Fbxo24 knockout mice exhibit disorganized mitochondrial coiling and abnormal head morphology.
source: While this paper was under review, another group reported analyses of Fbxo24 KO mice that exhibit not only disorganized mitochondrial coiling but also abnormal head morphology (Li et al., 2024).
evidence: Statement cites concurrent work by another group.

claim: Differences in Fbxo24 knockout phenotypes between studies may be due to different mouse genetic backgrounds.
source: The differences from our study may be due to different mouse genetic backgrounds.
evidence: Speculation about phenotypic differences.

claim: FBXO24 mediates the degradation of MIWI via K48-linked polyubiquitination.
source: The other group showed that FBXO24 mediates the degradation of MIWI via K48-linked polyubiquitination (Li et al., 2024).
evidence: Statement cites findings from another group's work.

claim: FBXO24 may be involved in the degradation of multiple proteins including IPO5 to support proper spermiogenesis.
source: FBXO24 may be involved in the degradation of multiple proteins including IPO5 to support proper spermiogenesis.
evidence: Inference from multiple substrate interactions.

claim: Numerous RNP granules accumulate in sperm flagella when FBXO24 is depleted.
source: In conclusion, we reveal that numerous RNP granules accumulated in sperm flagella when FBXO24, which is related to the UPS, was depleted.
evidence: Summary of main finding from TEM and other data.

claim: Small numbers of RNP granules are found even in control spermatozoa.
source: Small numbers of the RNP granules were found even in the control, suggesting that the ability to generate the granules is present in WT testes but may be suppressed by FBXO24.
evidence: Observation from TEM data.

claim: The ability to generate RNP granules is present in wild-type testes but may be suppressed by FBXO24.
source: Small numbers of the RNP granules were found even in the control, suggesting that the ability to generate the granules is present in WT testes but may be suppressed by FBXO24.
evidence: Inference from presence of granules in both WT and KO.

claim: FBXO24 can be a key molecule for understanding the formation and function of aberrant RNP granules in male fertility.
source: FBXO24 can be a key molecule for understanding the formation and function of the aberrant RNP granules in male fertility.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from study findings.

claim: Amino acid sequences and expression patterns of FBXO24 are conserved between species.
source: Because amino acid sequences and expression patterns of FBXO24 are conserved, FBXO24 may also play similar roles in human testes.
evidence: Statement based on sequence alignment and expression data.

claim: FBXO24 may play similar roles in human testes.
source: Because amino acid sequences and expression patterns of FBXO24 are conserved, FBXO24 may also play similar roles in human testes.
evidence: Inference from conservation data.

claim: This research may lead to development of new approaches to infertility treatment and nonhormonal male contraceptives.
source: Our research may lead to development of new approaches to infertility treatment and nonhormonal male contraceptives.
evidence: Speculation about potential applications.

claim: FBXO24 is involved in the degradation of IPO5, disruption of which may lead to the accumulation of abnormal RNP granules in sperm flagella.
source: These results suggest that FBXO24 is involved in the degradation of IPO5, disruption of which may lead to the accumulation of abnormal RNP granules in sperm flagella.
evidence: Summary conclusion from ubiquitination, interaction, and phenotype data.

claim: The primary cause of infertility in Fbxo24 knockout mice is impaired sperm migration in the female reproductive tract due to reduced sperm motility.
source: These results suggest that the primary cause of infertility is impaired sperm migration in the female reproductive tract due to reduced sperm motility.
evidence: Inference from motility, migration, and fertility data.
